summary: The plan halted at the expand stage when the SQL statement containing a $$-quoted PL/pgSQL function definition failed to execute. The runner reported a syntax error at the $$ delimiter, indicating the SQL string was not correctly formatted or escaped for PostgreSQL parsing.
revision_notes: The previous plan's expand stage failed because the SQL string for the trigger function began with '$$', causing PostgreSQL to misinterpret the dollar-quote syntax. This revision splits the trigger setup into separate single-statement SQL strings starting with CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION (not $$), resolving the syntax error.

stages.description: Add the customer_note column and create a trigger to sync note to customer_note.
sql: ALTER TABLE account_user ADD COLUMN customer_note TEXT NULL;
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION sync_note_customer_note() RETURNS TRIGGER AS $$ BEGIN NEW.customer_note := COALESCE(NEW.note, NEW.customer_note); RETURN NEW; END; $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;
CREATE TRIGGER sync_note_customer_note BEFORE UPDATE ON account_user FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION sync_note_customer_note();

stages.description: Copy existing note values into customer_note so the new app can read the most recent data.
sql: UPDATE account_user SET customer_note = note WHERE note IS NOT NULL;

stages.description: Deploy the new application version using a state-only migration (no SQL executed by the new Django migration).
Retire the old application version so only the new version handles database operations.
Remove the old note column now that the old app is retired.
sql: ALTER TABLE account_user DROP COLUMN note;
